analysis.one_liner: Blocks EPA carbon emission rules for power plants until carbon capture is proven feasible.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2012 with one sponsor and 13 cosponsors, the bill never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the EPA from finalizing any carbon dioxide emission standard for existing or new fossil-fuel power plants until at least three of four named federal officials published a report finding that carbon capture and storage is technologically and economically feasible for those plants [S2][S3]. Until that finding, no carbon rules for coal- or gas-fired generating units could take effect [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies and coal-fired electric utilities. The bill would have removed the threat of federal carbon emission limits on their plants and products for as long as officials declined to find carbon capture feasible, sparing them the cost of compliance while keeping coal burning unrestricted [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal mining companies and coal-fired utilities

how_it_helps.text: Would prohibit the EPA Administrator from finalizing any carbon dioxide performance standard for any existing or new fossil fuel-fired electric generating unit under section 111 of the Clean Air Act [S3].

Would require at least three of four designated officials — the EIA Administrator, the Comptroller General, the Director of the National Energy Technology Laboratory, and the Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology — to find carbon capture and storage technologically and economically feasible before any rule could be finalized [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public, through carbon emissions from power plants that would remain unregulated until the feasibility finding was made — a finding that, if never published, would keep the standards blocked indefinitely [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via delayed emission cuts

drawbacks.text: Because the bill covers both existing and new fossil-fuel generating units, it would have blocked standards for plants already operating, not just future construction [S3].

The gate depends on three of four officials making a feasibility finding; if that finding never came, carbon standards for power plants would be postponed without limit, leaving power-plant emissions unaddressed [S2][S3].

Supporters' premise — that no standard should rest on capture technology not yet commercially demonstrated — is a real policy dispute, but this bill resolved it by removing EPA's authority to act at all rather than by setting a deadline or funding for demonstration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have lowered near-term compliance costs for coal-dependent utilities and possibly electricity rates in coal-reliant regions, but it did so by suspending federal carbon limits on power plants with no end date. The main benefit flows to a concentrated industry; the main cost — continued power-plant emissions — is spread across the public. As a trade-off, it weighs toward the industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power Subcommittee, which held one hearing, but the committee never reported it and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative David McKinley introduced the bill on July 24, 2012, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power [S5].
The subcommittee held a hearing on September 20, 2012, but no markup or floor vote followed [S5].
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, with the bill still in committee; it never received a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public interest in EPA's authority to set carbon standards for power plants stayed intact, since nothing was enacted; the coal industry gained nothing from the bill's death beyond the status quo. Because the bill served a concentrated industry, its failure left ordinary people no worse off than before it was introduced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA kept its carbon-rule authority; coal gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: Of the 13 cosponsors, 7 were Democrats and 6 were Republicans — a coalition built around coal and fossil-energy states rather than party lines [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have blocked EPA carbon standards for fossil-fuel power plants, the main demand source for coal, until carbon capture was found feasible — protecting coal demand from regulation [S2][S3]. Ordinary people bear the postponed emissions and air-quality costs.
Would have spared existing and new coal generating units the cost of complying with carbon dioxide performance standards under the Clean Air Act [S3].

The bill makes a CCS feasibility finding the trigger for regulation but provides no funding or mandate for it; delaying the standards also delays the compliance pressure that would drive CCS deployment [S2][S3].
